$comment: UK Trade Secrets / Confidential Information - the Trade Secrets Regulations 2018's incorporation of the common-law breach of confidence test. Fresh research this session. Coco v A N Clark (Engineers) Ltd [1968] FSR 415 predates the neutral-citation system and Find Case Law's coverage, so it is verified via the citing-judgment method through Jones v IOS (RUK) Ltd [2012] EWHC 348 (Ch), fetched live and directly from Find Case Law, which quotes it directly by pinpoint page reference.

authorities.name: Trade Secrets (Enforcement, etc.) Regulations 2018, regs 2-3
authorities.date_note: Made under the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018, implementing Directive (EU) 2016/943, now retained/assimilated UK law post-Brexit. The text verified this session is the current in-force version; the page notes one pending, not-yet-applied future amendment (SI 2026/723) that does not affect the text quoted here.
authorities.proposition: Defines a 'trade secret' as information that is secret, has commercial value because it is secret, and has been subject to reasonable steps to keep it secret (reg 2). Critically, the Regulations do not create a free-standing unlawful-acquisition test separate from the common law: acquisition, use, or disclosure of a trade secret is unlawful where it constitutes a breach of confidence in confidential information (reg 3(1)), and a trade secret holder may seek breach-of-confidence remedies in addition to, or as an alternative to, the Regulations' own remedies where they provide wider protection (reg 3(2)-(3)). The Regulations are chiefly procedural (limitation, confidentiality-preserving orders, damages) rather than a substantive re-codification of the cause of action.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly this session, cross-checked across three separate page fetches (as-made text, current in-force text, and the individual regulation pages) all consistent.

authorities.name: Coco v A N Clark (Engineers) Ltd
authorities.proposition: The classic three-element test for breach of confidence absent a contract: (1) the information itself must have the necessary quality of confidence about it; (2) it must have been imparted in circumstances importing an obligation of confidence; and (3) there must be unauthorised use of the information to the detriment of the party who communicated it. This is the common-law test reg 3(1) of the Trade Secrets Regulations 2018 incorporates as the substantive definition of unlawfulness.
authorities.verification_note: Predates the neutral-citation system and Find Case Law's coverage entirely - no direct primary-source fetch was attempted for that reason. Verified via Jones v IOS (RUK) Ltd & Anor [2012] EWHC 348 (Ch) (below), which quotes Megarry J's three-element test directly at paragraph 40 with a pinpoint page reference ('at 419'), independently re-fetched and re-confirmed a second time, plus corroboration via Thomson Reuters Practical Law's case citator entry.
